questions.q: Among $10^{-9} \mathrm{~g}$ (each) of the following elements, which one will have the highest number of atoms? Element : $\mathrm{Pb}, \mathrm{Po}, \mathrm{Pr}$ and Pt
questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.solution:
$\text { No. of atoms }=\frac{\text { Massin } g}{\operatorname{Molar} \operatorname{Mas}(\mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol})} \times \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{A}}$
Therefore for the same Mass element having the least Molar mass will have the higher no. of atoms.
- $\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{Po}}=209$
- $\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{Pr}}=141$
- $\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{Pb}}=207$
- $\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{Pt}}=195$

questions.q: What would be the molality of 20% (mass/mass) aqueous solution of $KI$ ? (molar mass of $KI = 166gmol^{- 1}$ )
questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.solution:
Molality $= \dfrac{Molesofsolute}{weightofsolvent\left(g\right)} \times 1000$
$100gm$ of solution contains $20gmKI$
So, the moles of $KI= \dfrac{20}{166}$
Weight of solvent $= 100 - 20 = 80gm$
Molality $= \dfrac{20 \times 1000}{166 \times 80}$
$= 1.51Molal$

questions.q: When a hydrocarbon $A$ undergoes complete combustion it requires $11$ equivalents of oxygen and produces $4$ equivalents of water. What is the molecular formula of $A$?
questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.solution:
By using the formula of combustion analysis:

${C}_{x}{H}_{y} + \left(x + \dfrac{y}{4}\right){O}_{2} \to {CO}_{2} + \dfrac{y}{2}{H}_{2}O$

Given,~\left(x + \dfrac{y}{4}\right)a = 11a$

$x + \dfrac{y}{4} = 11$

\left(\dfrac{y}{2}\right)a = 4a$

$y = 8$,

then~$x + \dfrac{8}{4} = 11$

$x = 11 - \dfrac{8}{4}$

$x = 9$

Formula~$= {C}_{9}{H}_{8}$

questions.q: The first and second ionisation enthalpies of a metal are $496$ and $4560kJmol^{- 1}$, respectively. How many moles of $HCl$ and ${H}_{2}S{O}_{4},$ respectively, will be needed to react completely with $1$& mole of the metal hydroxide?
questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.solution:
Ionization Enthalpy& values indicate& that the metal belongs to $I^{st}$ group, since the second ionization enthalpy~is very high.
(Q - only one valence electron)
Metal hydroxide will be of the type, $MOH$.

$\mathop{\text{MOH}}_{\left(1\text{mol}\right)} + \mathop{\text{HCl}}_{\left(1\text{mol}\right)} \to \text{MCl} + {H}_{2} \text{O}$

$\text{MOH} + \dfrac{1}{2} {H}_{2} {\text{SO}}_{4} \to \dfrac{1}{2} {M}_{2} {\text{SO}}_{4} + {H}_{2} \text{O}$

$( 1\text{mol} ) \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \text{mol}\right) So, one mole of $HCl$~is required to react with one mole of~$MOH$.

So, \dfrac{1}{2} mole of ${H}_{2} {\text{SO}}_{4}$~is required to react with one mole of~$MOH$.$

questions.q:
A metal chloride contains $55 . 0 %$ of chlorine by weight. $100mL$ vapours of the metal chloride at STP weigh $0 . 57g$. The molecular formula of the metal chloride is

(Given: Atomic mass of chlorine is $35 . 5u$)
questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.solution:
Let the formula of metal chloride be ${MCl}_{x}$

Mass of $100mL$ of vapours of ${MCl}_{x}$~at~STP $= 0 . 57g$

The mass of substance which occupies 22400 ml of volume at STP is molar mass(M)

$∴ \dfrac{100 \times M}{22400} = 0 . 57$

$∴$~Molar mass of ${MCl}_{x} = 127 . 68g{mol}^{– 1}$

The mass percentage of chlorine$= \dfrac{massofchlorine}{massofthecompound} \times 100$

$%$~of~$Cl = \dfrac{35 . 5x \times 100}{127 . 68} = 55$

$⇒ x = 2$

$∴$~Formula of metal chloride is~${MCl}_{2}$

\because N_{1} V_{1}=N_{2} V_{2}

questions.q: The ammonia  \left({NH}_{3}\right)$~released on quantitative reaction of $0.6g$ urea  \left({NH}_{2}CON{H}_{2}\right)$~with sodium hydroxide  \left(NaOH\right)$& can be neutralized by$
questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.solution:
${NH}_{2}{CONH}_{2} + 2NaOH \to 2{NH}_{3} + {Na}_{2}{CO}_{3}$

By, stoichiometry, $1mol$ of urea gives $2mol$~${NH}_{3}$

Moles of urea =$= \dfrac{0 . 6gm}{60gm / mol} = 0 . 01mol$

So, $0 . 01$ mole urea produce $0 . 02$ mole~${NH}_{3}$

To neutralize ammonia~$HCl$~is required

${NH}_{3} + HCl \to {NH}_{4}Cl$

By equation, it is clear that $1mol$ of ammonia is neutralized by 1mol of~$HCl$.

So, $0 . 02mol$ of ammonia neutralized by $0 . 02mol$ of~$HCl$

$∴ MoleofHCl = 0.02mole$

$EquivalentofHCl = normality \times volume = 0 . 2N \times 100mL = 0 . 02equivalent$

As $n$-factor of~$HCl$~is $1$, so $numberofequivalents = numberofmoles = 0 . 02moles$

Hence, option $3$ is correct.

questions.q: A $100mL$ solution of ${CH}_{3}{CH}_{2}MgBr$ on treatment with methanol produces $2 . 24mL$ of a gas at STP. The weight of gas produced is____mg (nearest integer)
questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.solution:
In the above reaction the Ethyl group of grignard reagent acts as a strong base.

As per the stoichiometric equation the number of moles of methanol is equal to the number of moles of ethane.

Volume of methanol=Volume of ethane$=2 . 24ml$

Hence, number of moles of ethane

$n = \dfrac{2 . 24 \times {10}^{- 3}}{22 . 4} = {10}^{- 4}$

Weight of the gas= Number of moles$\times$~Molecular mass

$W = n \times M$

$= {10}^{- 4} \times 30 = 3mg$

questions.q: If $5$ moles of ${BaCl}_{2}$~is mixed with $2$ moles of ${Na}_{3}{PO}_{4},$ the maximum number of~moles of ${Ba}_{3}\left({PO}_{4}\right)2$formed is _________& (Nearest integer)
questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.solution:
The balanced chemical equation for the reaction between ${BaCl}_{2}$ and ${Na}_{3}{PO}_{4}$ is:

$3{BaCl}_{2} + 2{Na}_{3}{PO}_{4} \to {Ba}_{3} ( {PO}_{4}{)}_{2} + 6NaCl$

$5$~moles of barium chloride will require~$\dfrac{5 \times 2}{3} = 3 . 3$~moles of sodium phosphate.

Here, sodium phosphate is the limiting reagent.
$2$~moles of sodium phosphate produce~$1$~mole of barium phosphate.

Thus,$2$~moles of sodium phosphate will produce$1$~mole of barium phosphate.

Hence, the maximum no. of moles of ${Ba}_{3} ( {PO}_{4}{)}_{2}$that can be formed is one& mole.

questions.q: Number of moles of methane required to produce $22g{CO}_{2 ( g )}$ after combustion is $x \times {10}^{– 2}$ moles. The value of $x$ is
questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.solution:
${CH}_{4} + 2{O}_{2} \to {CO}_{2} + 2{H}_{2}O$

Gram molecular mass of ${CO}_{2} = 12 + 2 ( 16 ) = 44g / mol$

From the reaction, it is clear that $1$ mole of methane on complete combustion produces $44g$ ($1$ mole) of carbon dioxide.

Therefore moles of ${CH}_{4}$ required to produce $22g$ of ${CO}_{2}$ are:

$= \dfrac{1}{44} \times 22 = 0 . 5mol = 50 \times {10}^{- 2}mol$

Hence, $m = 50$
